title: Fruit and Vegetable Scraps Could Boost Health — Study
paragraphs: When people prepare fruit and vegetables, they often throw away the peels, skins, stalks and seeds. However, according to new research from King's College London, these discarded parts may actually be among the most nutritious.

The study, which was led by Dr. Rachel Gibson and published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, analyzed 12 common types of fresh produce. The researchers discovered that in 10 of them, the parts that are usually thrown away contained significantly higher levels of dietary fiber than the parts that people normally eat.

Some of the differences were striking. For instance, the skin and core of a pineapple contained roughly five times as much fiber as the flesh. Similarly, the skin and seeds of butternut squash provided 9.25 grams of fiber per 100 grams, which is nearly a third of the amount of fiber that adults are recommended to eat each day.

The researchers also found that these overlooked parts made up between 25% and 48% of the total weight of the produce. According to Gibson, this means people are discarding a significant portion of the fruit and vegetables they buy, which she said is not only a nutritional loss, but also a financial one.

Fiber is an important part of a healthy diet, yet many people do not eat enough of it. Eating these parts of fruit and vegetables could therefore be a simple and inexpensive way to increase fiber intake while also reducing food waste.

Interestingly, when the researchers served a tasting menu that included these ingredients and asked diners what would encourage them to eat such parts, the extra fiber turned out to be a stronger motivation than the environmental benefits.

Nevertheless, the researchers emphasized that the study had some limitations. It did not test whether eating these parts actually improves people's health. In addition, more research is needed into pesticide residues and other possible contaminants that may be present on skins and peels. Other recent scientific reviews have likewise concluded that, although fruit peels contain a variety of beneficial compounds, further research is required.
